community_evidence.text: I don't normally upload cats or dogs, but I'm uploading this one because I found it in association with a live mouse, which I also [observed here](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233922482). When the photo was taken, the mouse was still underneath the cat; it seemed to be under the cat's hips. I thought the cat was sitting strangely, so I approached it to see if it was injured and needed veterinary care, but the cat didn't appreciate my approach and got up and left, revealing the mouse. The cat seemed to be in good condition. I didn't see a collar. Unknown if this is feral, escaped/lost, or an outdoor pet; at the very least, it's a competent hunter, so probably not a recently escaped indoor cat. It was not friendly towards me as I approached; it flicked its tail consistently and did not sniff my outstretched hand. It tolerated me until I got closer than an extended arm's reach.
No wounds or net marks; nor does it seem in poor condition. Photo by John McCallum.

Southern Sea Otter grooming it’s fur. Sea otters groom themselves meticulously to maintain the insulating quality of their dense fur, which is essential for survival in cold waters. My favorite Southern Sea Otter (Enhydra lutris ssp. nereis) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=41860&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1 Female with Scarred Nose: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/165516431 Male showing Teeth: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/164818190 Praying: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/175683723 Typical Tail Position: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151550648 Southern Sea Otter (Enhydra lutris ssp. nereis) is a Pacific Ocean marine dwelling mammal in the Mustelids (Mustelidae) family that grows 3.5-4.5 ft (up to 1.5 meters) long. Northern Sea Otters are a lot larger than Southern Sea Otters, so they are probably the largest weasel. Unlike most marine mammals, the sea otter's primary form of insulation is an exceptionally thick coat of fur, the densest in the animal kingdom. Although it can walk on land, the sea otter is capable of living exclusively in the ocean. Sea Otters are usually seen resting while wrapped up in floating Kelp beds, floating on their backs cracking open seafood with small rocks, eating, sleeping, preening thick fur, carrying one pup, or teaching the pups to dive and find food. Sea Otters eat a variety of shellfish, sea urchins, and especially red fat innkeeper worms in Elkhorn Slough. They do not go after fish. The range of Southern Sea Otters is usually south of San Francisco CA and north of the Channel Islands in southern California. Conservation Status: Vulnerable and threatened (T) in United States (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service). The numbers of sea otters are holding steady, but the gene pool is very small because their numbers were radically reduced during the fur trade for ladies fashion :-( California Department of Fish and Wildlife: http://sibr.com/mammal

community_evidence.text: This whale had part of a pectoral fin and possibly its lower jaw entangled in a gill net. Per an update from Island Packers, it was able to free itself: “Tow Boat U.S. and Vessel Assist, carrying a seasoned response team, was able to confirm that humpbacks in the immediate area were free of gear and none appeared entangled. After closely reviewing and comparing all the photos and timestamps, it was clear that we had an almost complete documentation of the whale freeing itself from the netting. The team noted a distinct white mark on the upper right tail fluke from both the entangled whale and freed whale and they all believed, based on the photos and the whale’s behavior of frequent breaching, pec slapping, and tail lobbing, it had successfully freed itself from the gear and is now swimming free!”
